questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
A few aspects were crucial for me when I had to choose my study destination: 
- Interesting courses and a large selection of courses taught in English to be sure that I could choose from many courses if I would not get my first priorities. 
- A city with a large student community. I don't find that Copenhagen is a student friendly city so I thought it would be fun to live and study in a city with a large student community. 
- Good opportunity to find decent housing.
- Not too far from Denmark as it was important for me to travel by sustainable means of transportation and for my partner to come and visit me. 
- The nature! I like to do outdoor activities and furthermore nature offers alot of free or cheap activities and access to nature is something I really miss when in Copenhagen.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Overall, I have been very satisfied with my exchange experience in Bergen. I have enjoyed the nature, made new friends from all of Europe and travelled Norway. 

A few things could have been better though: 
- One of the reasons I choose UiB was that they had a course in energy and climate law in the course overview at the time I had to apply for exchange with UCPH. When I had to apply for courses in december 2022, the course was not available anymore. I think it should be visible which courses the exchange students can choose between at the time we have to start to apply for exchange. 
- The teaching of the courses I had was not very interesting. It was pretty old school lectures with no interactions between professor and students. In the end a very few students participated in the lectures.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. There was a lot of email contact from the international coordinators from UiB and they replied quickly to questions.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There were introduction days, and additionally the people working at the information centre at the Faculty of Law were very helpful.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
The student welfare organisation Sammen guarantees housing for exchange students in one of their student housings in the city. Most students are offered a shared room at the Fantoft student housing a bit outside the city centre. This was also the case for me. I rejected the offer as I could not see myself in a shared room without the possibility to take time for myself. However, I met a lot of students who stayed in a shared room and was happy with it - and it is a very cheap housing option; around 4000 NOK including utilities.
I ended up creating a profile on
hybel.no
and with my knowledge of the Copenhagen housing market i expected the worst. Though, it was super easy to get in contact with several student who wanted to rent out a room in a shared apartment. I ended up living in a shared apartment with a Norwegian girl in the city centre. The location was perfect and living with a local was an excellent opportunity to get to know the Locals and speak the language. It was way more expensive that the student housing offered by Sammen, but with Erasmus funding, the Governments support (SU) and some private funding, I found that it worked really well for me - and it was still cheaper than what a similar room would have costed in Copenhagen.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
That you have to put more effort into meeting people and make friends. I went to alot of events arranged by the local ESN - in the beginning they had events almost everyday so it was just to show up and start interacting with other people. 

In general it was easy to connect as all exchange students are there to meet new people and are not busy with existing obligations, such as seeing family and working.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Compared to Copenhagen, it was easy to find housing and the housing available was rather cheap.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I can't remember, but it was digital and very easy. UiB provided a lot of information and also sent reminders when close to a deadline.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: They responded quickly to any kind of question by email. And also after arrival, it was easy to get help in person by showing up at the faculty's information centre which was open every day between 8 and 16.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got the classes I wanted and I didn't change courses during the semester.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: You will have all the help available you need - just ask questions.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The lectures were rather boring as no interaction between student and professor where expected and the students were not expected to prepare for the lectures. For one of my courses we didn't even have an overview of the topics covered so it was hard to know how to prepare. This resultet in quite a disapoiting academic level of the lectures.

On the other hand, the exams were not easy. You really had to be well prepared to do good at the exams.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: See my answer above.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: See above, I think I covered it.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- European Human Rights Law (20 credits) 
- International Climate Law (10 credits)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
None of the above courses unfortunately. I was not satified by the academic level. 
Climate law was super interesting but the professor did not go into details and was more interested in talking about himself and how he was flying around Europe to give lectures and his love for red wine and steaks... almost a statement not to be willing to be part of the solution of the climate crisis.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None i can remember. I kept my sim-card from my danish supplier so no extra charges than what I was used to.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Norway is in general an expensive country - especially alcohol and dining out is expensive. Food can be expensive depending on your diet, but it was not as expensive as I thought (also in the view of the value of the NOK being very weak during my stay). 

My experience was that as a Danish student I had quite a good economy compared to exchange student from other countries, which meant that I could have spent much more money than I ended up doing, because my friends did not have the money to dine out in restaurants and do expensive activities.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: For an outdoor and ski enthusiast like me, Norway is one of the best countries to live in.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: A lot of associations, however I didn't join any of them as I quickly became part of a group of friends where we planned the activities ourselves.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Skiing, hiking (an important part of norwegian culture), sailing, kayaking, swimming and sauna and so on.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Skiing and hiking. So many opportunities. Also travel north to see the Northern Lights (if you are lucky).

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Seek private housing with one or more local roomies instead of staying in one of the student housings.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None - the Norwegians are very friendly people, can keep a bit to themselves, maybe even more than us Danes, but I think we understand them very well.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The way they made use of their amazing nature! Everyone - from young kids to the elderly went on hikes and stayed in shape.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Bergen is a quite small city. If you are looking for a bustling metropol, go another place. I definitely missed some of the city life I'm used to in CPH. 
- Don't be fooled by the relatively low academic requirements at the lectures. The exams are not easy. 
- Bring your outdoor equipment - in my opinion your stay will become much better if you enjoy the nature like the Norwegians.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Covered above

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Being in the nature - I miss the mountains.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I don't think I experienced any challenges that was not easy to overcome. Of course I missed friends, my boyfriend and family at home, but it was my own choice to study abroad for a while, and I did not regret at any point.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Enjoy the rain! It rains a lot - learn to have fun outside eventhough  the weather is showing off and find likeminded friends.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
